section.title: Java Core — OOP, Collections & Concurrency
section.subtitle: Collection implementations deep-dive, iterators, comparable vs comparator, enum, singleton, bean lifecycle, threads, synchronization, streams, Optional and more.

topics.title: Collections — Lists (ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack, ArrayDeque)
topics.learn: When to use which list — capacity, thread-safety, performance.

python.definition: Python has ONE list type covering all cases — dynamic array, not thread-safe. deque from collections for queue/stack behaviour. No capacity control.
python.code:
from collections import deque

lst = [1, 2, 3]          # dynamic, auto-grows
lst.append(4)           # amortised O(1)
lst.insert(0, 0)        # O(n) — shifts all
lst.pop()              # O(1) from end
lst.pop(0)             # O(n) from front!

d = deque([1,2,3])      # fast both ends
d.appendleft(0)         # O(1)
d.popleft()             # O(1)

java.definition: ArrayList: dynamic array, ~50% growth (10->15->22...), NOT thread-safe — default choice. LinkedList: nodes, O(1) insert at ends, more memory, rarely used. Vector: legacy, synchronized (thread-safe), 100% growth. Stack: Vector subclass, LIFO. ArrayDeque: resizable array, faster than Stack/LinkedList for stacks/queues. Capacity: ArrayList initial 10.

topics.title: Collections — Sets (HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet)
topics.learn: Unique-element collections — capacity, ordering, null rules.

python.definition: set = unordered unique items (hash table). dict.fromkeys or set() — no capacity control, allows None. frozenset = immutable version.
python.code:
s = {1, 2, 3, 3}        # {1, 2, 3} — dup removed
s.add(4); s.remove(1)
print(None in s)          # can hold None

# Ordered variant: dict keys preserve insertion order
ordered = dict.fromkeys([3, 1, 2])   # {3:None, 1:None, 2:None}

# Sorted: use sorted() (returns list)
print(sorted(s, reverse=True))

java.definition: HashSet: hash table, cap 16, grows ~double, NOT thread-safe, allows ONE null, unordered. LinkedHashSet: HashSet + insertion-order linked list, allows null. TreeSet: Red-Black tree, NO capacity, sorted order, NO null allowed, extra methods: first(), last(), headSet(), tailSet(), descendingSet(), subSet().

topics.title: Collections — Maps (HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable)
topics.learn: Key-value stores — capacity, thread-safety, ordering, null rules.

python.definition: dict = hash table, insertion-ordered (3.7+), keys must be hashable, allows one None key. No thread-safe variant built-in (use threading.Lock).
python.code:
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
d["c"] = 3
del d["a"]
print(d.get("x", 0))    # default value
print(d.keys(), d.values(), d.items())

# Ordered: dict IS insertion-ordered
# Sorted: dict(sorted(d.items()))
# Thread-safe: wrap with a Lock

java.definition: HashMap: cap 16, ~75% load factor triggers resize, NOT thread-safe, allows ONE null key + many null values. LinkedHashMap: HashMap + insertion/access order. TreeMap: Red-Black tree, keys sorted, NO null keys. Hashtable: LEGACY — synchronized (thread-safe), NO null key/value, cap 11. ConcurrentHashMap = modern thread-safe choice.
java.code:
Map<String,Integer> hm = new HashMap<>();      // cap 16
Map<String,Integer> lhm = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // insertion order
Map<String,Integer> tm = new TreeMap<>();      // sorted keys
Map<String,Integer> ht = new Hashtable<>();    // legacy, sync
Map<String,Integer> chm = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // thread-safe!

hm.put("a", 1); hm.put(null, 0);   // null key OK
ht.put(null, 1);                     // NullPointerException!
tm.put(null, 1);                     // NullPointerException!

// ConcurrentHashMap for multi-threaded access

topics.title: Iterators — Iterator, ListIterator, Enumeration & Legacy
topics.learn: Traversing collections; old legacy classes and their replacements.

python.definition: iter() creates iterator; next() advances; for-loop uses it internally. iterators support remove() (since 3.x). list_iterator? — iter() only goes forward; reversed() goes backward.
python.code:
lst = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(lst)          # create iterator
print(next(it))         # 10
print(next(it))         # 20

# for-loop = sugar for iterator
for x in lst: print(x)

# Remove during iteration
for x in lst[:]:        # iterate over COPY
    if x == 20: lst.remove(x)
# or use list comprehension to filter

java.definition: Iterator<T>: hasNext()/next()/remove() — FORWARD only, all collections. ListIterator<T>: adds hasPrevious()/previous()/add()/set() — LISTS only, bidirectional. Enumeration<T>: LEGACY forward-only, can't remove — replaced by Iterator. Legacy->modern: Vector->ArrayList, Stack->ArrayDeque, Hashtable->HashMap, Enumeration->Iterator.

topics.title: Comparable vs Comparator
topics.learn: Two ways to define sort order — natural vs custom.

python.definition: sorted() takes key= function — equivalent of Comparator. __lt__ in a class = Comparable (natural ordering). No interface needed.
python.code:
students = [("Priya", 90), ("Sam", 85), ("Amy", 95)]

# key= = Comparator equivalent
by_name = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[0])
by_marks = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True)

# __lt__ = Comparable equivalent
class Student:
    def __init__(self, marks): self.marks = marks
    def __lt__(self, other): return self.marks < other.marks

sorted([Student(90), Student(85)])

java.definition: Comparable<T>: class implements compareTo() — ONE natural ordering, can't change at runtime. Comparator<T>: separate class/lambda — MULTIPLE custom orderings, use for different sorts. sort() uses Comparable; sort(comparator) uses Comparator.

topics.title: Enum — Constants with Behaviour
topics.learn: Enumerations: constructors, methods, values(), ordinal(), valueOf(), abstract methods.

python.definition: Python 3.11+ has enum.Enum/IntEnum — named constants with optional methods. No ordinal/valueOf builtins — use list(Enum) and Enum['NAME'].
python.code:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2
    BLUE = 3

    def describe(self):          # methods allowed
        return f"color-{self.name}"

print(Color.RED.describe())
print(list(Color))              # all values
print(Color['RED'])             # by name
print(Color.RED.value)          # 1
print(Color.RED.name)           # 'RED'

java.definition: enum = fixed set of constants. Can have constructor (private), fields, methods, abstract methods (each constant implements). Built-ins: values() -> all constants array, ordinal() -> index, valueOf("NAME") -> constant by name.

topics.title: Singleton Pattern
topics.learn: Ensuring only ONE instance of a class — eager, lazy, thread-safe.

python.definition: Module itself acts as singleton (import once). __new__ can enforce single instance; or use a metaclass / module-level instance.

java.definition: Eager: instance created at class load (static field). Lazy: created on first getInstance(). Thread-safe: synchronized method or Bill Pugh (static inner class — best practice, lazy + thread-safe without sync).

topics.title: Bean Lifecycle
topics.learn: Spring bean creation phases: instantiate, populate, initialize, destroy.

python.definition: Python has no bean container — but Django app loading follows similar phases: import models -> populate -> ready(). __init__ ~ instantiate, __init_subclass__ ~ initialize.
python.code:
# Django AppConfig.ready() runs once at startup
class MyAppConfig(AppConfig):
    def ready(self):
        # 'initialize' phase — connect signals, setup
        pass

# Object lifecycle in plain Python:
obj = MyClass()      # __new__ (instantiate) + __init__ (populate/init)
del obj              # __del__ (~destroy)
# No standard 'destroy' hook — use context managers:
with resource() as r: ...   # __exit__ = cleanup

java.definition: Spring bean lifecycle: 1) Instantiate (new), 2) Populate properties (@Autowired/DI), 3) Initialize (@PostConstruct / InitializingBean / init-method), 4) Ready for use, 5) Destroy (@PreDestroy / DisposableBean / destroy-method).

topics.title: Thread Life Cycle
topics.learn: States: NEW -> RUNNABLE -> RUNNING -> WAITING/BLOCKED/TIMED_WAITING -> TERMINATED.

python.definition: Python threads (threading.Thread) have similar states but GIL limits true parallelism for CPU work. start() begins, run() contains logic, join() waits.
python.code:
import threading, time

def worker():
    print("running")
    time.sleep(1)
    print("done")

t = threading.Thread(target=worker)  # NEW
t.start()                            # -> RUNNING
t.join()                             # main waits -> TERMINATED

# States via t.is_alive()
# No explicit BLOCKED/WAITING states visible

java.definition: NEW (created, not started) -> RUNNABLE (start() called, waiting for CPU) -> RUNNING (executing on thread) -> WAITING (wait()), TIMED_WAITING (sleep()), BLOCKED (waiting for lock) -> TERMINATED (run() ends or stop()).

topics.title: Thread Communication — wait/notify/sleep/join, Race Condition, synchronized
topics.learn: Inter-thread communication and preventing race conditions.

python.definition: threading: wait()/notify()/notify_all() via Condition; sleep() pauses; join() waits for thread. Lock/RLock prevent race conditions; GIL helps but doesn't eliminate races.
python.code:
import threading, time

lock = threading.Lock()
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    with lock:            # synchronized block equivalent
        counter += 1

# Race condition: counter += 1 without lock
# can lose updates when threads interleave

t1 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
# time.sleep(0.1) = pause thread
# Condition().wait()/notify() = wait/notify

java.definition: wait() releases lock & waits for notify()/notifyAll(). sleep(ms) pauses (doesn't release lock). join() waits for thread death. Race condition = shared data corrupted by concurrent access — fixed by synchronized (method or block) or locks.

topics.title: Java Streams — Source, Intermediate & Terminal Operations
topics.learn: Stream pipeline: source -> intermediate ops -> single terminal op.

python.definition: No streams — generators + itertools.chain/map/filter give lazy pipelines. List comprehensions are eager equivalent.
python.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# Pipeline = comprehension (eager)
result = [x*x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]

# Lazy pipeline = generator expression
result = (x*x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)

# itertools for advanced pipelines
import itertools
evens = itertools.filterfalse(lambda x: x % 2, nums)
squares = map(lambda x: x*x, evens)

java.definition: Stream pipeline: SOURCE (list.stream(), Arrays.stream) -> INTERMEDIATE (map, filter, sorted, distinct — lazy, return new stream) -> TERMINAL (collect, forEach, reduce, count — triggers execution, returns value). Streams can't be reused after terminal op.

topics.title: Optional — Null-Safe Values
topics.learn: Java's Optional vs Python's None handling.

python.definition: None = null equivalent. No Optional wrapper — use `x or default`, `if x is not None`, or walrus. Type hints Optional[int] document nullable intent.
python.code:
name = None

# Safe access patterns
greeting = f"Hi {name}" if name else "Hi guest"
# or: name = name or "guest"

from typing import Optional
def find_user(id: int) -> Optional[dict]:
    return users.get(id)   # may return None

user = find_user(1)
if user is not None:
    print(user["name"])

java.definition: Optional<T> wraps a value that may be null — forces explicit handling. Methods: of(), ofNullable(), orElse(), orElseGet(), orElseThrow(), ifPresent(), map(), filter(). Never use Optional as field/param type (return types only).

topics.title: Wrapper Classes
topics.learn: Object equivalents of primitives: Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.

python.definition: Python has NO wrapper classes — int, str, bool ARE objects already. Everything is an object; no primitive/wrapper split.
python.code:
x = 10           # already an object
print(type(x))      # <class 'int'>
print(x.bit_length())  # methods on int!
print((10).to_bytes(2, 'big'))

# No Integer vs int distinction
# No boxing/unboxing needed

java.definition: Wrapper classes box primitives into objects: Integer, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Character, Byte, Short. Needed for collections (can't store primitives), generics, null values. Autoboxing/unboxing converts automatically.

topics.title: final Keyword & yield
topics.learn: final prevents modification; yield returns values from switch/generators.

python.definition: No final keyword — convention: UPPER_CASE for constants. yield = generator keyword (pause & return value). match/case has no yield.

java.definition: final variable = can't reassign; final method = can't override; final class = can't extend. yield = keyword in switch expressions returning a value (Java 14+).

topics.title: Dates & Times
topics.learn: Working with dates, times and durations in both languages.

python.definition: datetime module: datetime (date+time), date, time, timedelta (duration). strptime/strftime for parsing/formatting. zoneinfo for timezones.
python.code:
from datetime import datetime, date, timedelta

now = datetime.now()
today = date.today()

print(now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"))  # format
parsed = datetime.strptime("2024-01-15", "%Y-%m-%d")

future = today + timedelta(days=30)     # add duration
diff = future - today                    # timedelta
print(diff.days)

# timezones
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
now_est = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))

java.definition: java.time package (Java 8+): LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Duration, Period, DateTimeFormatter. Immutable, thread-safe — replaces old Date/Calendar.

topics.title: File Handling — Deep Dive
topics.learn: Reading/writing files, directories, paths — both languages.

python.definition: pathlib.Path = modern way: read_text(), write_text(), glob(), mkdir(). open() still works. os module for system ops.
python.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("data.txt")
p.write_text("hello")          # write
print(p.read_text())             # read
print(p.exists(), p.suffix)      # checks

for f in Path(".").glob("*.py"):  # find files
    print(f.name)

Path("newdir").mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Binary mode
p.write_bytes(b"\x00\x01")

# os for system-level
import os
print(os.getcwd(), os.listdir())

java.definition: java.nio.file.Files + Path.of() = modern. Files.readString/writeString/readAllLines. File class = legacy. try-with-resources for streams.

topics.title: Math Functions & Constants
topics.learn: pow, sqrt, round, floor, ceil, max, min, random.

python.definition: math module: pow, sqrt, floor, ceil, trunc, fabs, exp, log, sin/cos. round() = banker's rounding. random module for random. math.inf, math.pi constants.
python.code:
import math, random

math.pow(2, 10)        # 1024.0
math.sqrt(16)          # 4.0
math.floor(3.7)        # 3
math.ceil(3.2)         # 4
round(3.5)            # 4 (banker's: round(2.5)=2!)
math.trunc(3.9)        # 3
abs(-5)               # 5
max(1,2,3), min(1,2,3) # 3, 1
random.randint(1, 10)  # random int
random.random()       # 0.0-1.0
math.pi, math.e        # constants
math.isinf(float('inf'))

java.definition: Math class static methods: pow, sqrt, floor, ceil, round, abs, max, min, random. Strictfp for consistency. Math.PI, Math.E constants.
java.code:
Math.pow(2, 10)      // 1024.0
Math.sqrt(16)        // 4.0
Math.floor(3.7)      // 3.0
Math.ceil(3.2)       // 4.0
Math.round(3.5)      // 4 (half-up, NOT banker's!)
Math.abs(-5)         // 5
Math.max(1,2)        // 2 (only 2 args)
Math.min(1,2)        // 1
Math.random()        // 0.0-1.0
ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1,11) // random int
Math.PI, Math.E      // constants

topics.title: String Comparison
topics.learn: equals() vs ==, compareTo(), startsWith/endsWith/contains.

python.definition: == compares VALUE for strings. is compares IDENTITY (same object). .lower() before comparing for case-insensitive. compare via < > works lexicographically.
python.code:
a = "hello"; b = "hello"
print(a == b)        # True — value
print(a is b)        # True — interned (same object)

c = "hello " + "world"[:0]  # new object
print(a is c)        # False!

# Case-insensitive
print(a.lower() == "HELLO".lower())

# Ordering
print("apple" < "banana")  # True (lexicographic)

java.definition: == compares REFERENCE (same object in memory). equals() compares VALUE. compareTo() returns -1/0/1 for ordering. equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive.

topics.title: Loop Control — break, continue, else
topics.learn: Exiting/controlling loops; for-else in Python.

python.definition: break exits loop, continue skips to next. for...else / while...else runs else ONLY if loop completed WITHOUT break (like a 'no break' flag).

java.definition: break exits innermost loop; continue skips to next iteration; labeled break/continue exits OUTER loop. No for-else — use a boolean flag.

topics.title: Array/List Functions — map, filter, reduce equivalents
topics.learn: JS-style array functions (map/filter/reduce/forEach/find) in Java & Python.

python.definition: List comprehensions + built-ins cover everything: map(), filter(), reduce() (functools), any/all, sorted with key.
python.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# JS map -> comprehension or map()
squares = [x*x for x in nums]
squares = list(map(lambda x: x*x, nums))

# JS filter -> comprehension
evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]

# JS reduce -> functools.reduce
from functools import reduce
total = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums, 0)   # sum=15

# forEach -> for loop
for x in nums: print(x)

# find -> next()
first_even = next(x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)

# includes -> in operator
print(3 in nums)   # True

java.definition: Streams replace all JS array functions: map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach(), findFirst(), anyMatch(), noneMatch(), allMatch().

topics.title: HTTP Status Codes
topics.learn: 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500 — what each means and when to use.

python.definition: Django/DRF: return Response(data, status=201) or status.HTTP_201_CREATED. requests library: resp.status_code checks.
python.code:
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework import status

# Common codes:
# 200 OK — success (GET, PUT)
# 201 Created — resource created (POST)
# 204 No Content — success, no body (DELETE)
# 400 Bad Request — invalid input
# 401 Unauthorized — not logged in
# 403 Forbidden — logged in but no permission
# 404 Not Found — resource missing
# 500 Server Error — crash

return Response(student, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
return Response({"error": "invalid"}, status=400)

import requests
r = requests.get(url)
print(r.status_code)  # 200, 404, etc.

java.definition: Spring: ResponseEntity.ok(body), .status(HttpStatus.CREATED), or return ResponseStatusException. Same HTTP semantics.

topics.title: Relationships — One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-Many
topics.learn: How entity relationships map in Django ORM vs JPA.

python.definition: ForeignKey = many-to-one (student->course). OneToOneField = 1:1. ManyToManyField = n:n (auto junction table). related_name for reverse access.

java.definition: @ManyToOne (many side has FK), @OneToMany (inverse), @OneToOne, @ManyToMany (join table auto-created). mappedBy for inverse side. CascadeType for propagation.

topics.title: BODMAS — Operator Precedence Deep Dive
topics.learn: Exact order of operations with examples both languages execute.

python.definition: Precedence high->low: () [] {} -> ** (right-assoc) -> +x -x ~x (unary) -> * @ / // % -> + - -> << >> -> & -> ^ -> | -> comparisons -> not -> and -> or -> if-else -> lambda -> :=. Key gotcha: ** binds tighter than unary on LEFT.
python.code:
# BODMAS examples — verify yourself:
print(2 + 3 * 4 ** 2)     # 2 + 3*16 = 50
print((2 + 3) * 4 ** 2)   # 5 * 16 = 80
print(10 - 4 - 3)         # 3 — LEFT assoc!
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)        # 512 — RIGHT assoc
print(-2 ** 2)            # -4 — ** before unary!
print(not True == False)  # True — == before not
print(1 if True else 0)   # ternary lowest

# Java differences: / always true division for int?
# NO — Java int/int = int! Python / always float

java.definition: Precedence high->low: () [] . -> ++ -- unary + - ! ~ -> * / % -> + - -> << >> >>> -> < <= > >= instanceof -> == != -> & -> ^ -> | -> && -> || -> ?: -> = += etc. Multiplicative before additive; shifts before relational.
java.code:
// BODMAS — same order as math:
System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);      // 14
System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);    // 20
System.out.println(10 - 4 - 3);     // 3 (left assoc)
System.out.println(2 * 3 % 4);      // 2 (* and % same level, left)
System.out.println(1 << 2 + 1);     // 8 — + before <<!
System.out.println(5 > 3 && 2 < 4); // true
System.out.println(-2 * -3);        // 6

// GOTCHA: int division
System.out.println(7 / 2);          // 3 (int!)
System.out.println(7.0 / 2);        // 3.5
System.out.println(7 % 2);          // 1

topics.title: Checking Data Types at Runtime
topics.learn: How to inspect and verify types in both languages.

python.definition: type(x) returns the class; isinstance(x, cls) checks inheritance; issubclass for classes. Type hints don't enforce at runtime.
python.code:
x = 10
print(type(x))                    # <class 'int'>
print(isinstance(x, int))         # True
print(isinstance(x, (int, float))) # True — tuple of types

class Animal: pass
class Dog(Animal): pass
print(isinstance(Dog(), Animal))   # True — inheritance!

# Type hint (not enforced)
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int: return a + b
add("1", "2")  # still works — returns '12'!

java.definition: obj.getClass() returns runtime class; instanceof checks type (incl. subclasses); getClass() == Class.class for exact match. Compile-time types vs runtime types differ with polymorphism.
